items.title: Why the old report stays but the old maintenance goes
items.body:
`pastThreshod` is today minus `pastDays`. The maintenance loop returns early when `maintenance.from < pastThreshod`, and incidents check `createdAt` the same way. The reports branch has no such check; its comment says all unresolved reports are displayed. So a 60-day-old maintenance is dropped while a 60-day-old unresolved report stays on the timeline.

- *Both*: the maintenance threshold drops the old maintenance.
- *Neither*: reports are deliberately exempt from the threshold.
- *Only the maintenance*: it is the other way round.

excerpts.quote: we don't check threshold here because we display all unresolved reports

items.title: Kata 3 starts from a page that renders nothing while loading
items.body:
**Key: it returns null, so the user sees a blank page until data arrives.**

The status-reports page runs two client queries, one for the page and one for its reports. Its render function begins with `if (!statusReports || !page) return null;`. While either query is still loading, or if one fails, `data` is undefined and the component renders nothing at all. Kata 3's premise is exactly this: the dashboard should not show blank UI while the query state is unknown. Its test mocks a loading query and expects loading text.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Renders the layout's prefetched list*: the layout does prefetch, but the page still returns null whenever data is missing.
- *Throws to an error boundary*: nothing throws; it returns null.
- *An empty table with a message*: that would be an empty state, which the page does not have yet.

excerpts.quote: Page currently returns null if reports or page is absent
if (!statusReports || !page) return null;

items.title: Concept: building the public timeline, and guarding URLs
items.body:
The public status page shows a timeline of **events**: maintenances, incidents and status reports. `getEvents` in `packages/api/src/router/statusPage.utils.ts` builds that list. Read it slowly and make a table with one row per source (maintenances, incidents, reports) and these columns: how it is filtered by component or monitor, whether the 45-day threshold applies, and what `type`, `status` and `to` the event gets. Fill it in from the code, not from the workout's bullet list.

In `packages/api/src/router/statusPage.ts`, find where `statusReports` is sorted. A JavaScript comparator must return a negative number when `a` comes first, a positive number when `b` comes first, and zero for a tie, and it must be consistent. Check each branch of this comparator against that contract.

The SSRF guard in `packages/utils/src/ssrf.ts` stops the server from fetching internal addresses. Read `isBlockedIPv4`, `isBlockedIPv6`, `isBlockedHost`, and both `assertSafeUrl` functions. For each, list exactly what it inspects and what it ignores.

excerpts.quote: `getEvents` collects maintenances, incidents, and reports into a common event shape

items.title: Why a statuses filter on the tRPC list has no effect
items.body:
The router's input is `z.object({ period, order, pageId })`. A zod object schema strips keys it does not declare unless told otherwise, so `statuses` disappears during parsing. The router then always calls the service with `statuses: []`, `limit: 10_000` and `offset: 0`. In `listStatusReports` a status condition is added only when `input.statuses.length > 0`, so every status comes back. The workout predicts this test would fail today.

- *Only resolved*: the service supports the filter, but the router never passes it.
- *Zod throws*: an object schema strips unknown keys by default.
- *Capped at 100*: that limit belongs to the separate Connect handler; tRPC passes 10,000.

excerpts.quote: limit: 10_000, offset: 0, statuses: [],
if (input.statuses.length > 0) {

items.title: Why the hex IPv4-mapped loopback is blocked
items.body:
`isBlockedHost` sees a bracketed host and calls `isBlockedIPv6` with `::ffff:7f00:1`. That function handles the `::ffff:` prefix: it first tries the rest as a dotted IPv4, then splits the two hex groups `7f00` and `1`, rebuilds `127.0.0.1` from their bytes, and asks `isBlockedIPv4`, which blocks the 127 range. The comment explains why: Node's URL parser rewrites the dotted form into this hex form.

- *Only the dotted form*: the hex branch exists for exactly this input.
- *Every IPv6 literal*: public IPv6 addresses are allowed.
- *IPv6 skips the checks*: bracketed hosts go through `isBlockedIPv6`.

excerpts.quote: Node's URL parser converts ::ffff:127.0.0.1 to ::ffff:7f00:1 (hex form)

items.title: getEvents gets a unit test because it is computation over arrays
items.body:
**Key: it is a pure-ish helper that computes events over plain arrays.**

The layer table pairs each behaviour with the cheapest layer that can see it. `getEvents` takes lists of maintenances, incidents and reports plus a few ids and returns a list of events. It needs no database, router or HTTP request, so a unit test can call it with hand-built arrays and check the result directly. "Pure-ish" is an honest qualifier: the function also reads the current date for its age threshold.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A utility boundary guarding URLs*: that is the SSRF guard's row, tested as a utility.
- *Where workspace ownership lives*: that rule lives in the service, so it gets a service test.
- *Computing the public read model in statusPage.get*: that is a different row, tested at the router or integration layer.

excerpts.quote: `getEvents` is a pure-ish helper over arrays
Workspace ownership and transaction writes | Service test | Business rule lives in service

items.title: Why static components show no incidents
items.body:
All incident handling sits inside `if (componentType !== "static") { ... }`. A static component is a manual entry on the page with no monitor behind it, so the code skips incidents entirely, whatever monitor id is passed. The monitor filter and the 45-day threshold apply only inside that block.

- *All incidents from 45 days*: that is the behaviour for monitor-type components.
- *Only unresolved ones*: the block is skipped as a whole.
- *Only matching monitorId*: the filter never runs for a static component.

excerpts.quote: Static components don't have incidents

items.title: Why a monitoring update closes the range but stays degraded
items.body:
`getEvents` sorts a report's updates by date. If `report.status` is `"resolved"` it emits a `success` event. Otherwise it emits a `degraded` event whose `to` is the last update's date when that update's status is `resolved` or `monitoring`, and `null` otherwise. Here the report is investigating and the last update is monitoring, so the event is degraded and ends at that update.

- *Success*: only the report's own status `resolved` gives success.
- *Open with to null*: monitoring is one of the two statuses that set `to`.
- *No event*: an unresolved report with updates is included whatever its age, as long as it passes the component filter.

excerpts.quote: lastUpdate?.status === "monitoring" ? lastUpdate?.date : null,

items.title: expectAuditRow matches on four fields and reads through tx
items.body:
**Key: workspace id, action, entity type and entity id, read through the test's tx.**

In the skeleton, the test calls the service, then asks `expectAuditRow` for a row with `workspaceId: workspace.id`, `action: "thing.create"`, `entityType: "thing"` and `entityId: result.id`, passing `db: tx`. The helper reads the audit log for that workspace and entity and fails the test unless one row has the expected action. Because the whole test runs inside `withTestTransaction`, which never commits, the read must go through the same `tx` to see the row at all.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Only the entity id, from the committed database*: the test's writes are never committed.
- *A full row snapshot after commit*: the helper matches a few fields, and nothing commits.
- *The action name from a logging spy*: it queries the real audit table.

excerpts.quote: await expectAuditRow({ workspaceId: workspace.id, action: "thing.create", entityType: "thing", entityId: result.id, db: tx,
`expectAuditRow` asserts audit rows were written

items.title: withTestTransaction always rolls a test's writes back
items.body:
**Key: it wraps the test body in a transaction that always rolls the writes back.**

The helper opens a database transaction, runs your test body inside it with the transaction handle `tx`, and then throws a private `RollbackSignal` error. Throwing makes the transaction roll back; the helper catches that one error and returns your result. So every row the service wrote during the test disappears afterwards, whether the assertions passed or failed. That is why the service under test must be given `db: tx`: only reads through the same transaction can see its uncommitted rows.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Commits, then a teardown deletes by prefix*: nothing is ever committed.
- *Rolls back only when an assertion fails*: the rollback is unconditional.
- *Commits so later tests can reuse the rows*: tests must not depend on each other's writes; each test's writes vanish.

excerpts.quote: `withTestTransaction` wraps a test body and always rolls back writes
Wrap a test body in a transaction that always rolls back, so per-test

items.title: Why notifying on a plan without subscribers does nothing
items.body:
After loading the update and checking that it belongs to the caller's workspace, `notifyStatusReport` tests `ctx.workspace.limits["status-subscribers"]`. When it is false, the function simply returns: no dispatch, no error. The comment says this silent skip matches the existing email router. The workout asks whether that should be user-visible instead.

- *ForbiddenError*: that is thrown only when the update belongs to another workspace.
- *Dispatches anyway*: the plan check runs before `dispatchStatusReportUpdate`.
- *Queued for later*: there is no queue; the call just ends.

excerpts.quote: Plan does not enable subscribers

items.title: Assert an error message only when it is meant to be stable
items.body:
**Key: assert it only if stable, but avoid overfitting to a deliberately generic one.**

The router test already pins the error *code* (`NOT_FOUND`), which is the public contract a client branches on. A message can add value when its wording is stable and meaningful. But some messages are generic on purpose. Pinning such a message to the letter makes the test fail on harmless rewording, which is overfitting: the test checks an accident of the implementation instead of the behaviour.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Assert the full message every time*: that is exactly the overfitting the workout warns about.
- *Never assert the message*: the workout allows it when the message is stable.
- *Only in service tests*: the advice is about this router test; nothing says routers rewrite messages.

excerpts.quote: assert the error message if stable enough, but avoid overfitting if the message is intentionally generic.

items.title: The service's workspace-scoped query rejects the foreign page
items.body:
**Key: only the service queries the page by id and workspace, so the rejection lives there.**

`createStatusReport` looks the page up with a `where` that requires both the page id *and* the caller's workspace id. A page that belongs to another workspace simply is not found, and the service throws `NotFoundError` before inserting anything. Because that rule is written in the service, the service test is the most direct place to prove it; the router test only checks that the error reaches clients with the right tRPC code.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Router tests cannot build a caller*: they can; the router workout builds one with `createInnerTRPCContext`.
- *A database foreign key rejects the insert*: no insert happens; the lookup fails first.
- *requireScope enforces ownership*: it checks API-key and MCP scopes, not which workspace owns a page.

excerpts.quote: Why this belongs in service tests: the service owns the workspace page lookup
and(eq(page.id, input.pageId), eq(page.workspaceId, ctx.workspace.id)),

items.title: Which rows one status-report create writes
items.body:
Workout 1 lists the happy-path effects of `createStatusReport`: a `status_report` row, a `status_report_update` row (the initial update), a `status_report_to_page_component` row linking the affected component, and audit rows for both the report and the update. The audit rows are written with `emitAudit` inside the same transaction.

- *Update row only, audit later*: the link row is also written, and audit is not deferred.
- *Link row and one audit row*: both the report and the update are audited.
- *Subscriber notification rows*: notifying subscribers is the separate `notifyStatusReport` verb.

excerpts.quote: status_report_to_page_component row audit rows for report and update

items.title: Audit rows belong to the service, next to the writes they record
items.body:
**Key: audit is a service-owned side effect, tied to the domain writes it records.**

`createStatusReport` inserts the report and its first update, and in the same transaction calls `emitAudit` twice: once for `status_report.create` and once for `status_report_update.create`. Because audit is written by the service, next to the data it describes, every caller gets it: the dashboard, the API, MCP and Slack alike. That is why Kata 5's test checks the audit row in a service test, through the same transaction, rather than anywhere in the UI.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A dashboard feature*: the kata says the opposite: audit is not a UI feature.
- *Written later by a job*: the audit rows are emitted inside the create transaction.
- *A router concern*: the service emits them, so non-tRPC callers get audit too.

excerpts.quote: audit is not a UI feature; it is a service-owned side effect tied to domain writes.
`createStatusReport` emits audit rows for report create and update create

items.title: Five helpers, five kinds of caller for a service test
items.body:
**Key: user, API key, MCP, Slack and system-job actors.**

A `ServiceContext` tells a service verb which workspace it acts in and *who* is acting. The test map lists one helper per kind of caller: `makeUserCtx` (a dashboard user), `makeApiKeyCtx` (an API key, with scopes), `makeMcpCtx` (an MCP client, also with scopes), `makeSlackCtx` (a Slack user) and `makeSystemCtx` (a background job, named by `job`). Picking the right one lets a test check rules that depend on the actor, such as scope checks that apply to some actors and not others.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Inbound-webhook actors*: the map has no webhook constructor.
- *Admin and guest actors*: no such helpers exist; a user context carries only a user id.
- *OAuth-app actors*: API access is modelled with `makeApiKeyCtx`, not an OAuth app.

excerpts.quote: `makeUserCtx`, `makeApiKeyCtx`, `makeMcpCtx`, `makeSlackCtx`, and `makeSystemCtx` construct `ServiceContext` actors

items.title: Choosing and designing tests: the test map and the katas
items.body:
Two files in the lab are about *choosing and designing* tests rather than reading existing ones.

`docs/test-first-learning-lab/01-test-map.md` is the index. It lists the file globs where each kind of test lives, gives a table that matches behaviours to the layer that should test them, and maps the helpers that service tests are built from. Read the table one row at a time and open the code each row cites. For every row, ask why that layer, and not the one above or below it, is the right place.

`05-test-design-katas.md` holds five short exercises. Each starts from a feature premise and a list of existing facts with code cites, shows a test to write first, and ends with something to expect or decide. Before you read a kata's last line, predict it yourself from the cited code, then compare. Keep a note of anywhere your prediction and the kata disagree, and check the code to see who is right.

Finally, go back to the service and router workouts: their "practice extension" lines are exercises in the same spirit.

excerpts.quote: What To Test At Which Layer
Feature premise: dashboard should filter status reports by status.

items.title: Why the report comparator is inconsistent
items.body:
A comparator returns a negative number to put `a` first and a positive number to put `b` first. This one returns `-1` when `a` has no updates (correct: a goes first) and also `-1` when `b` has no updates, which again puts `a` first, the opposite of the comment's intent. The second branch should return `1`. Because the result depends on argument order, the comparator is inconsistent, and the final order depends on the engine's sort algorithm.

- *Returns 0*: 0 is returned only when both have no updates.
- *Throws*: the empty-array checks return before the last-update read.
- *Puts the empty report first*: -1 orders `a`, not `b`, first.

excerpts.quote: if (a.statusReportUpdates.length === 0) return -1; if (b.statusReportUpdates.length === 0) return -1;

items.title: Concept: status reports, from service verb to router
items.body:
A **status report** is a public incident write-up on a status page, with a series of updates. The service verbs live in `packages/services/src/status-report/`; the tRPC routers in `packages/api/src/router/` wrap them and translate their errors.

Read `create.ts` and list every step in order: the scope check, input parsing, the page lookup (note its `where`), the page-component validation, and anything that runs between that validation and the first insert. For each failure, note which error class is thrown. Then read `notify.ts`, list each condition it tests before `dispatchStatusReportUpdate`, and note what the function does when a condition fails.

Next, open `packages/api/src/router/statusReport.ts`:

- For `create`, note what the procedure returns and how it handles errors (follow `toTRPCError` into `service-adapter.ts`).
- For `list`, compare the zod input object with the object passed to `listStatusReports`. Then read `list.ts` to see how each field is used.

Finally, re-read workout 1 of the service file and the real test it cites to see which rows one create writes.

excerpts.quote: the service owns the workspace page lookup

items.title: Start here: learning OpenStatus by reading its tests
items.body:
OpenStatus is an open-source uptime monitor with public status pages. This checkout is the monorepo itself, with a study library in `docs/`. This quest uses the **test-first learning lab**: `docs/test-first-learning-lab/`. Its idea is that a test is the most precise description of what code does, so you learn a module by reading its tests and then writing the next one.

Read in order:

1. `01-test-map.md`: which kinds of tests exist and where.
2. `02-service-test-workouts.md`: status reports in `packages/services`.
3. `03-router-test-workouts.md`: the same feature through the tRPC routers in `packages/api`.
4. `04-public-page-and-utils-tests.md`: the public status page helpers and the SSRF guard in `packages/utils`.

The workouts mix real test excerpts with code marked *illustrative fake*. Always open the real file a workout cites and check the behaviour yourself.

items.title: Why pageComponentId wins over monitorId
items.body:
The maintenance filter checks `if (pageComponentId)` first and returns its match. Only when `pageComponentId` is falsy does it try `monitorId`, and when neither is given it keeps every maintenance. The comment calls monitorId the backward-compatibility fallback. The reports filter uses the same order.

- *monitorId alone*: it is the fallback, not the first choice.
- *Either one*: the branches return before the next is tried, so there is no OR.
- *Both at once*: there is no AND either.

excerpts.quote: prioritize pageComponentId, fallback to monitorId for backward compatibility

items.title: Why a foreign page id surfaces as NOT_FOUND
items.body:
The page lookup filters on both `page.id` and `page.workspaceId`, so a page from another workspace is not found, and the service throws `NotFoundError("page", input.pageId)`. The router catches it and calls `toTRPCError`, which maps a ServiceError with code `NOT_FOUND` to a `TRPCError` with code `NOT_FOUND`. The router test asserts exactly this code.

- *FORBIDDEN*: the service never reveals that the page exists elsewhere.
- *BAD_REQUEST*: the page id is a valid number, so input parsing passes.
- *INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR*: the service throws before any insert.

excerpts.quote: if (!page_) throw new NotFoundError("page", input.pageId);

items.title: Why components from another page cause a conflict
items.body:
`createStatusReport` first loads the page by id and workspace, then calls `validatePageComponentIds`, which checks the ids against the workspace and reports which page they belong to. If that page is not null and differs from `input.pageId`, the service throws `ConflictError` naming both pages. The components are legitimately the workspace's own, so this is a conflict between two inputs, not an ownership failure.

- *NotFoundError*: the page itself was found; the components are validated by workspace.
- *ForbiddenError*: the components belong to the same workspace.
- *Linked anyway*: the throw happens before the insert.

excerpts.quote: if (validated.pageId !== null && validated.pageId !== input.pageId) { throw new ConflictError(

items.title: Kata 2: the design decision picks the test layer
items.body:
**Key: it depends on whether the fix is a service, a post-commit job or router code.**

Today the dashboard creates a report and then, in the browser's `onSuccess` callback, calls a second mutation to send the notification. If that callback never runs, for example because the tab was closed, nobody is notified. Kata 2 sketches a test for a combined service, but then asks the real question: should this be a new service, a post-commit job, or a router orchestration? Each answer puts the code in a different place, so the test that proves it belongs at a different layer. Deciding the design comes before choosing the test.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A dashboard component test*: the whole point is to stop depending on the browser.
- *Always a router test*: router orchestration is only one of the three options.
- *A utility test*: dispatching to subscribers is not a pure helper over arrays.

excerpts.quote: Design question: should this be a new service, a post-commit job, or a router orchestration? The answer changes the test layer.
Feature premise: report notification should not depend on browser `onSuccess`.

items.title: Why a hostname pointing at a private IP passes
items.body:
Read the body of `assertSafeUrl`: it parses the URL, rejects non-HTTP protocols, and calls `isBlockedHost(parsed.hostname)`. `isBlockedHost` compares the name with a blocklist and checks it only if it is a raw IP literal. Nothing calls a DNS resolver, so a public-looking name whose record points to `10.0.0.5` passes. The docblock and the test section header both claim DNS resolution; the code does not do it, and no test uses a name that resolves to a private address.

- *Blocked after a lookup*: no lookup happens.
- *An allowlist*: the guard uses blocklists, not an allowlist.
- *Invalid URL*: the URL parses fine; only parsing failures throw that.

excerpts.quote: if (isBlockedHost(parsed.hostname)) {

items.title: A read-only MCP actor is refused like a read-only API key
items.body:
**Key: ForbiddenError, as requireScope checks mcp actors the same way as apiKey ones.**

Write verbs such as `createStatusReport` call `requireScope(ctx, "write")` first. `requireScope` returns immediately for user, Slack, system and other actor types, which have their own trust boundaries. For `apiKey` and `mcp` actors it checks the held scopes, and a context holding only `read` fails the check with `ForbiddenError`. The existing test proves this for `makeApiKeyCtx`; the extension repeats it with `makeMcpCtx`, which should behave identically.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Success, mcp is not checked*: the check applies to both `apiKey` and `mcp`.
- *NotFoundError*: the scope check runs before any lookup, and scopes do not hide pages.
- *Every non-user actor is rejected*: Slack and system actors pass, and an mcp actor holding `write` passes too.

excerpts.quote: since `requireScope` treats `mcp` like `apiKey`
if (actor.type !== "apiKey" && actor.type !== "mcp") { return; }
